title: Safe staffing and skill mix
blurb: Recognise NICE nursing red flags, escalate unsafe staffing and skill mix, and use evidence to make a basic business case.
question: A 28-bed ward needs 40 hours of registered nurse time on a late shift, but only 30 hours are available. Is this a nursing red flag, and what should happen?

teach.body: Safe staffing means having enough staff, with the right skills, to meet the nursing needs of the patients actually on the ward. NICE safe staffing guideline SG1 (2014) says patients' individual nursing needs (acuity and dependency) are the main factor in deciding how many staff are needed. There is no single nurse-to-patient ratio for all adult wards. In plain English: count the needs, not just the beds, and check the skills as well as the heads.
teach.cite: NICE SG1 (2014) Box 1, rec 1.5.3; proficiency P6.2

items.label: patients per RN on day shifts linked to increased harm
registered nurses on a ward in any shift: red flag
delay in pain relief: red flag
shortfall of RN time, whichever is reached first

head: Red flag
In practice
rows: A dose missed because no one was free
Vital signs not done as per care plan
RN time shortfall over 8 h or 25%
Fewer than 2 RNs on the ward
teach.caption: Other red flag events may be agreed locally.
NICE SG1 recs 1.4.2–1.4.4. Deal with the patient's need at once as well as escalating.

teach.h: Skill mix matters as much as numbers
teach.body: A full rota can still be unsafe if the skills are wrong. Delegate only within the other person's competence (Code 11.1), work within your own competence and ask for help (Code 13), and raise concerns immediately if asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training (Code 16.2). Registered nurse tasks such as IV medicines and assessment of a deteriorating patient cannot be handed to an untrained healthcare assistant, so a skill mix gap must be escalated.

teach.caption: Safe nursing indicators include falls, pressure ulcers, medication errors and patient-reported experience (Box 3).

teach.body: Proficiency P7.12 asks nurses to develop a basic business case for additional care funding using finance, resources and safe staffing evidence. Set out the problem, the evidence (recorded red flags, safe nursing indicators such as falls or pressure ulcers, patient feedback), the options including doing nothing, their costs and benefits, and how success will be measured. Keep patient information anonymised.
teach.cite: Proficiency P7.12; NICE SG1 rec 1.4.4, Box 3; Code 5

teach.h: Worked scenario: Sister Joy on a medical ward
teach.body: On a late shift Joy's ward needs 40 hours of registered nurse time but has 30. The 10-hour shortfall is more than 8 hours, so it is a red flag. Mr Ito has waited 40 minutes for analgesia, a second red flag. Joy gives his analgesia now, escalates both red flags to the site manager straight away, redistributes work and records the events. Over three months she uses the recorded red flags and falls data to support a business case for an extra twilight nurse.

teach.text: The RN shortfall red flag is more than 8 hours OR more than 25% of the required time, whichever is reached first. On a shift needing 15 hours, 11 hours or less available is already a red flag even though the gap is under 8 hours.

items: Staffing follows patients' nursing needs; there is no single ratio, but over 8 patients per RN by day is linked to harm.
Red flags: missed medicines, pain relief over 30 minutes late, missed observations, missed rounding, RN shortfall, fewer than 2 RNs.
A red flag needs an immediate escalation response by the RN in charge, and recording.
Check skills as well as numbers; escalate a skill mix gap (Code 11.1, 16.2).
Records of red flags and safe nursing indicators are the evidence for a business case.

summary: You can now recognise the NICE SG1 nursing red flags, calculate an RN shortfall, and escalate unsafe staffing or skill mix immediately while meeting patients' needs. You can also use recorded evidence to build a basic business case for more resources.

A.q: Which of the following is a nursing red flag in NICE safe staffing guideline SG1?
options: A patient waiting 15 minutes for a call bell answer
One healthcare assistant on sick leave
Pain relief delayed by more than 30 minutes
A ward with two empty beds at midnight
A.why: SG1 Box 2 lists a delay of more than 30 minutes in providing pain relief as a nursing red flag, alongside missed medicines, missed observations, missed intentional rounding, RN shortfall and fewer than 2 RNs.

whyNot.0: A call bell wait is not one of the SG1 Box 2 red flags, although local flags may be agreed.
whyNot.1: One HCA absence is not in itself a red flag; the flags focus on RN time and missed care.
whyNot.3: Empty beds reduce demand and are not a red flag.

A.q: At the start of a night shift, a ward has one registered nurse and three healthcare assistants. What should happen?
options: Proceed, as the total number of staff is four
Escalate now: fewer than 2 RNs is a red flag
Review it at the morning safety huddle
Ask the HCAs to cover the second RN's usual tasks
A.why: SG1 Box 2: fewer than 2 registered nurses present on a ward during any shift is a red flag, which should prompt an immediate escalation response (rec 1.4.3).

whyNot.0: Total headcount does not replace the need for registered nurse skills.
whyNot.2: A red flag needs immediate escalation, not review the next morning.
whyNot.3: Registered nurse tasks cannot be delegated beyond the HCAs' competence (Code 11.1).

A.q: According to NICE SG1, who should make the immediate escalation response when a nursing red flag occurs?
options: The registered nurse in charge
The ward's healthcare assistant
The patient's consultant
The trust's chief executive
A.why: SG1 rec 1.4.3: a nursing red flag event should prompt an immediate escalation response by the registered nurse in charge, for example allocating additional nursing staff.

whyNot.1: HCAs should report concerns, but SG1 places the escalation response with the RN in charge.
whyNot.2: Consultants are informed about clinical concerns, but staffing escalation sits with the nurse in charge.
whyNot.3: Senior leaders review establishments; the immediate response is the RN in charge's.

B.q: A shift needs 24 hours of registered nurse time; 17 hours are available. Is this a nursing red flag under SG1?
options: No, because the shortfall is less than 8 hours
No, because a red flag needs both criteria met
Yes, because the shortfall is more than 25%
Yes, because every shortfall counts as a red flag
B.why: Shortfall = 24 − 17 = 7 hours, which is 29% of 24. SG1 sets the red flag at more than 8 hours or 25%, whichever is reached first, so the 25% limit is breached.

whyNot.0: The 8-hour limit is one test; the 25% limit is reached first here.
whyNot.1: The criteria are alternatives: whichever is reached first triggers the red flag.
whyNot.3: Small shortfalls below both thresholds are not red flags.

B.q: A student asks what NICE SG1 says about nurse-to-patient ratios on adult wards. What is the most accurate answer?
options: A fixed ratio of 1 nurse to 6 patients applies
No single ratio; over 8 per RN by day is linked to harm
A ratio of 1 to 8 applies day and night
Ratios are set locally by each healthcare assistant team
B.why: SG1 rec 1.5.3: there is no single ratio for all acute adult wards, but evidence links a registered nurse caring for more than 8 patients on day shifts to increased risk of harm, which should prompt close monitoring and action.

whyNot.0: SG1 does not set a fixed 1:6 ratio.
whyNot.2: SG1 does not set a fixed day-and-night ratio; the over-8 evidence relates to day shifts.
whyNot.3: Establishments are set by managers based on patients' needs, not by HCA teams.

B.q: A bank healthcare assistant arrives to fill a registered nurse gap. Two patients in that bay need IV antibiotics and one has a rising NEWS2. What should the nurse in charge do?
options: Give the bay to the HCA with a list of the IV doses
Ask the HCA to record NEWS2 and give the IV doses
Leave the IV doses until the next shift's registered nurse
Cover the RN tasks herself and escalate the skill mix gap
B.why: Safety depends on skill mix as well as numbers. IV medicines and assessment of deterioration cannot be delegated to an HCA (Code 11.1), so the RN tasks must be covered by a registrant and the gap escalated (SG1; Code 25.1).

whyNot.0: A list does not make IV administration within the HCA's competence.
whyNot.1: The HCA can record observations, but giving IV doses is outside their competence.
whyNot.2: Delaying antibiotics risks harm and could itself be a red flag (missed medicines).

C.q: Mid-shift, Zoe finds that hourly observations for Mrs Dale have not been done for 3 hours because of staffing, and Mr Price has waited 45 minutes for pain relief. What is the most appropriate sequence?
options: Do the observations and analgesia, then escalate and record
Record both as red flags first, then do the care
Escalate to the matron and wait for extra staff before acting
Ask Mr Price to wait while she completes all the ward's observations
C.why: Both are SG1 red flags (missed vital signs, pain relief delayed over 30 minutes). Patients' immediate needs come first, then the red flags are escalated immediately and recorded (SG1 recs 1.4.3–1.4.4; Code 1.2, 16.1).

whyNot.1: Recording before care delays the care both patients need now.
whyNot.2: Escalation is needed, but the patients' care cannot wait for extra staff.
whyNot.3: He has already waited longer than the red flag threshold; delaying further increases harm.

C.q: A surgical ward nurse is asked to cover a level 2 high-dependency unit, where she has no training, for the whole shift. What should she do?
options: Raise her concern now and agree safe support
Accept and do her best, as staffing is short
Accept and ask the unit's HCA to guide her
Refuse and go home, as it is outside her job contract
C.why: Code 16.2: raise concerns immediately if asked to provide care beyond your experience and training. Code 13.3: ask for help when an action is beyond competence. She should escalate and agree a safe arrangement, such as working under a competent nurse with suitable patients.

whyNot.1: Working beyond competence without support puts patients at risk.
whyNot.2: An HCA cannot provide the registered oversight needed for high-dependency care.
whyNot.3: Leaving abandons patients and staff; the concern should be raised and resolved.

C.q: A ward manager is preparing a basic business case for an extra twilight registered nurse. Which evidence will be most persuasive?
options: Staff opinions that the ward feels busy in the evening
Recorded red flags, falls and pressure ulcer data, with costs
A comparison with the staffing on the busiest ward in the trust
Named patient stories describing their poor experiences
C.why: SG1 recommends recording red flag events and safe nursing indicators (such as falls and pressure ulcers) to inform staffing decisions. A business case sets objective evidence against options, costs and benefits (P7.12), with anonymised data (Code 5).

whyNot.0: Opinions are useful context but are not objective evidence.
whyNot.2: Another ward's staffing does not reflect this ward's patients' needs.
whyNot.3: Identifiable patient stories breach confidentiality; anonymised feedback is appropriate.

reteach.title: Count needs, not beds
reteach.question: Two wards both have 28 beds. Why might one need far more nurses than the other?

blocks.body: One ward may have people with delirium, end-of-life care, high risk of deterioration or needing one-to-one care; the other may have people who are mostly independent. SG1 says these patient needs drive staffing. Red flags are the warning lights that the staff available today cannot meet today's needs, and the nurse in charge must act on them at once.

blocks.h: Is the RN shortfall a red flag?

blocks.text: Escalating a red flag never replaces the care itself: give the overdue pain relief and do the missed observations, then escalate and record.

explain.body: Unplanned omission of medicines; pain relief delayed over 30 minutes; vital signs not done as per care plan; intentional rounding delayed or missed; RN shortfall over 8 hours or 25%; fewer than 2 RNs on a shift.

test.q: A patient's 4-hourly observations in the care plan were not done for 8 hours because the ward was short-staffed. How should this be viewed?
options: As acceptable on a busy shift
As a matter for the next audit
As a red flag needing escalation
As a medicines management error to report
test.why: Patient vital signs not assessed or recorded as outlined in the care plan is a nursing red flag (SG1 Box 2), prompting immediate escalation by the RN in charge.

whyNot.0: Missed observations are a red flag precisely because they indicate unsafe staffing.
whyNot.1: Red flags need an immediate response, not deferral to an audit.
whyNot.3: This is missed monitoring, not a medicines error.

explain.body: Shortfall = required RN hours minus available RN hours. It is a red flag if it is more than 8 hours or more than 25% of the requirement, whichever comes first. Example: 40 hours required, less than 32 available is a red flag.

test.q: A shift needs 40 hours of RN time. Below what number of available hours does SG1 class it as a red flag?
options: 36 hours
34 hours
32 hours
30 hours
test.why: SG1 gives this example: if a shift requires 40 hours of RN time, a red flag occurs if less than 32 hours is available (a shortfall of more than 8 hours).

whyNot.0: A 4-hour shortfall is below both thresholds.
whyNot.1: A 6-hour shortfall is below both thresholds.
whyNot.3: 30 hours would be a red flag, but the threshold is crossed below 32 hours.

explain.body: Check that the people on duty have the skills patients need. Delegate within competence (Code 11.1) and raise concerns at once if asked to work beyond your competence (Code 16.2).

test.q: Which Code standard requires a nurse to raise concerns straight away if asked to provide care beyond her experience and training?
options: Code 11.1
Code 16.2
Code 21.1
Code 5.4
test.why: Code 16.2: raise your concerns immediately if you are being asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training.

whyNot.0: Code 11.1 is about delegating within the other person's competence.
whyNot.2: Code 21.1 is about refusing gifts, favours or hospitality.
whyNot.3: Code 5.4 is about sharing information when safety overrides confidentiality.

explain.body: Keep records of on-the-day staffing assessments and red flags (SG1 rec 1.4.4). With safe nursing indicators (falls, pressure ulcers, medication errors, patient experience), they show the need. Add options, costs, benefits and measures.

test.q: Why does NICE SG1 recommend keeping records of red flag events?
options: To identify staff for disciplinary action
To replace the need for routine incident reporting
To give to patients on discharge
To inform future staffing establishments
test.why: SG1 rec 1.4.4: keep records of on-the-day assessments and red flag events so they can inform future planning of ward staffing establishments or other action.

whyNot.0: Red flags reflect staffing against need, not individual misconduct.
whyNot.1: Incidents are still reported through the trust's system linked to LFPSE.
whyNot.2: Red flag records are for staffing governance, not discharge information.
